div.p: In a multi-core platform, resources, such as memory banks and buses, are mostly shared among all cores for power, performance, and cost reasons. The access interference on the shared resources poses a major challenge on the analysis of real-time properties, but can be alleviated if task data partition onto memory banks is applied with care. In this paper, we consider to schedule RAS (resource access sporadic) tasks onto a platform consisting of homogeneous cores and capacity-limited memory banks. According to our observation, we should avoid internal data spreading among the memory banks for a task while advocate external data spreading among memory banks for a given task set. We propose a two-phase algorithm with (4 + ρ + 3(2γ+1) γ ) speedup factor and (γ + 1) memory augmentation factor, where γ > 0 and ρ ≥ 1. The derived adjustable resource augmentation factors can be useful in terms of system synthesis and schedulability. Moreover, under the premise that a given task set is feasible, we devise a bi-section approach that can derive a schedulable solution requiring the least amount of memory augmentation. According to our experiment results, the proposed algorithm significantly outperformed the state-of-the-art algorithm [15] in terms of schedulability test even when memory augmentation is prohibited.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In response to the "power wall" problem, the multicore design has been proposed and shown effective in reducing percore power consumption and improving thermal dissipation. Recently, as the number of cores within a chip keeps growing, we are now entering a "many-core" era. Examples of many-core platforms are Kalray MPPA-256 [8], STHORM [2], and so forth. By investigating these platforms, we can find that the many-core platforms are mostly grouped into islands, in which homogeneous cores and high-performance SRAM (referred as local memory in the sequel) resides. One of the reasons behind such a design is to mitigate the interference on accessing the resources shared among cores, while resources, such as memory banks and buses, are shared among cores for power, performance, or cost concerns. Though the island-based design in hardware can bound the resource access interference moderately in the short term, it is inevitably an issue as the number of cores keeps scale in the long run. Specifically, the interference on shared memory access poses a major challenge, but might be alleviated if task data partition onto memory banks is applied with a proper algorithmic design.

Traditionally, real-time analysis is conducted by bounding the WCET of a single task executed in isolation and, then, performing schedulability test on top of the WCETs of a given task set. Though it may be sensible for single-processor platforms, it inevitably introduces more pessimism in the analysis for multi-core platforms due to the competition of other shared resources and potentially task suspension on cores [18]. When the considered platform is assumed time-compositional [11], [21], different task models with separately bounded execution time on different components are proposed, such as the superblock execution model [19], the M/C (memory-computation) model [17], and the RAS (resource access sporadic) model [12]. The superblock execution model considers that the execution of a superblock is composed of a data acquisition phase, a local execution phase, and a data replication phase. Likewise, the M/C model consists of a memory access phase and an execution phase. The two models make strong assumptions on the phases of a task and, thus, limits their applicability. On the other hand, the RAS task model bounds the total CPU execution time and the total resource access time separately without making assumptions on the time points to send memory access requests.

In the literature, efforts have been made to investigate multi-core real-time scheduling with joint management of the computing units and memory allocation [5], [4], [6]. For a given task set, the work [5] endeavors to minimize the required SPM memory size, while the work [4] focuses on the minimization of the required island number. However, over-pessimism in schedulability analysis may be introduced in the above work due to sticking to a single WCET value as an execution time upper bound for a task. On the other hand, on top of the RAS task model, the work [12] proposes a symmetric response-time analysis, in which a core-centric perspective and a shared-resource-centric perspective are employed to bound the response time of a task separately. Nevertheless, how memory access interference can be alleviated by proper data allocation among memory banks, which can be accessed in parallel, remains a challenging issue. The work [15] provides not only real-time analysis on a detailed memory model but a memory-bank partitioning heuristic. However, the memory banks considered in their algorithm are assumed unlimited capacity and, thus, its applicability may be limited in practice.

In this paper, we consider to schedule RAS tasks onto a platform consisting of homogeneous cores and capacitylimited memory banks. We explore partitioned fixed-priority scheduling for constrained-deadline tasks, and rectify the symmetric real-time analysis to adapt to the considered multi-bank platform. Two observations can be drawn from an exploratory speedup factor analysis for careless memory bank partitioning: First, we should limit the maximum number of banks among which the data requested within each memory access segment of a task may spread. Second, we should endeavor to spread the data allocation of different tasks within a given task set among banks. Stemming from the observations, we devise a two-phase memory partitioning algorithm with memory augmentation consideration in mind. We yield that the speedup factor of the proposed algorithm is (4 + ρ + 3(2γ+1) γ ) when each memory bank is augmented at most (γ + 1) times, where γ > 0 and ρ ≥ 1. The adjustable nature of the derived CPU speedup and memory augmentation factors can be useful from two different perspectives: In terms of system synthesis, we can help system developers to understand the trade-off between performance and hardware costs. On the other hand, in terms of schedulability, we could derive a schedulable solution requiring the least amount of memory augmentation under the premise that the given task set is feasible. To achieve this, a bi-section algorithm is further proposed and should be employed together with the two-phase algorithm. In the experiment, we conducted extensive simulations of different types of task sets and compare the experiment results with that of the state-of-the-art partitioning heuristic proposed in [15]. According to our experiment results, the proposed algorithm significantly outperformed the state-ofthe-art algorithm in terms of schedulability test even when memory augmentation is prohibited.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II defines the system model and the considered problem. The employed symmetric real-time analysis is detailed and rectified for the considered platform in Section III. In Section IV, we propose a two-phase partitioning algorithm with a bounded and adjustable resource augmentation factor, and a bi-section algorithm to yield a schedulable solution requiring the least amount of memory augmentation. We validate the proposed two-phase algorithm in Section V and conclude this paper in Section VI.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL AND DEFINITION
div.p: In Section II-A, we detail the characteristics of the considered task and platform models. On top of that, a problem definition is provided in Section II-B, while the idea of resource augmentation, the core technique applied to the later algorithm design, is explained in Section II-C.

div.head: A. Platform and Task Models
div.p: As shown in Figure 1, we consider a platform which consists of M homogeneous cores and coupled with P single-port memory banks. A memory bank is essentially constituted by rows and columns of memory cells, a row decoder, and a column decoder. The decoders are used to locate the memory cells of interest, while a memory cell is the place to store data. Examples of a memory cell could be a bi-stable flip-flop in SRAM. We refer interested readers to the book [13] for a comprehensive study of memory architectures. Different banks of memory can be accessed in parallel, whereas the access parallelism within a bank depends on the number of exported ports. Nonetheless, parallelism expansion by increasing the number of exported ports comes at the expense of chip size increasing and the chance of access conflict within a bank. Thus, in this work, we restrict our attention on bank-level parallelism by considering single-port memory banks, each of which contains B blocks of memory.

In the considered platform, we assume that the access path from a core is connected to each and every memory bank arbiter. Readers interested in on-chip interconnections are recommended to refer to the work [16]. Each of the memory bank arbiters enforces a fixed-priority policy, by which the arbiter grants the access right to the memory request assigned the highest priority on the spot. A memory request is served in a non-preemptive fashion, and the upper bound of the processing time for a memory request is denoted as η. During the execution of a task, several memory access segments may be issued, where each segment is composed of consecutive memory access requests. In contrast to the nonpreemptive nature of a memory request, a memory access segment is preemptable after a request is finished. In this work, we assume that the data access demand of a task in execution is served by direct memory access (DMA) units and, thus, the cores can be freed to execute other ready tasks.

Bank-level parallelism can be further exploited by applying different address mapping policies. The interleaved address mapping policy spreads the memory address of a memory request across memory banks in hopes of achieving higher memory throughput. However, despite its improvement in average-case performance, chances are the memory latency might be significantly increased when multiple tasks executed on different cores access the same banks simultaneously. Thus, in terms of worst-case guarantee in a real-time system, employing the interleaved policy might result in unnecessarily pessimistic real-time characteristics. In contrast, the blocked address mapping policy restricts a dedicated memory bank to be accessed by a memory request of a task, one at a time. In effect, the blocked policy may avoid excessive memory latency of a single memory request when compared with that of the interleaved policy.

In this paper, we consider a set of n independent sporadic real-time task set T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , • • • , τ n }, each of which is preemptive and of RAS (resource access sporadic). We characterize an RAS task τ i by a predetermined 7-tuple (m i , C i , A i , a j i , T i , D i , σ i ): m i denotes the number of memory blocks required for the task τ i ; C i denotes the upper bound of the total execution time for τ i on a computing core; A i denotes the upper bound of the time spent on local memory access for τ i without any interference; a j i denotes the upper bound of the time spent on local memory access for each memory block 1 ≤ j ≤ m i of τ i without any interference; T i denotes the minimum inter-arrival time of τ i ; D i denotes the relative deadline of τ i ; and σ i denotes the maximum number of resource access segments. In this work, we consider tasks are prioritized in a deadline-monotonic order.

After the task data is partitioned onto memory banks, we further characterize an RAS task τ i by a 2-tuple (A i , σ i ) on each memory bank . The 7-tuple can be derived by analyzing the program of an RAS task beforehand, and the 2-tuple can be determined at the time of memory bank partitioning. Specifically, A i denotes the upper bound of the time during which τ i spent on local memory access to the memory bank without any interference; and σ i denotes the maximum number of resource access segments on the memory bank . A i is determined by the sum of the memory access time upper bound of the memory blocks allocated to the bank . We assume that P =1 A i ≤ ρA i . Relations between σ i and σ i will be further discussed in Section III-C.

div.head: B. Problem Definition
div.p: In what follows, we discuss constraints and assumptions to the input parameters of a task set. Provided no memory interference on memory banks, the worst-case execution time of task τ i is considered C i + A i . We assume that C i + A i ≤ D i for each task τ i in the given task set. In addition, the number of memory blocks, m i , for any task τ i is allowed to be larger than the memory capacity B of a single memory bank, whereas the sum of memory blocks of a taskset, τi∈T m i , should be not more than P • B. Otherwise, the task set is inherently infeasible if any of the above mentioned real-time constraint or memory block constraint is violated. Given a task set, we say that it is an implicit-deadline task set if D i = T i holds for each task τ i , and a constrained-deadline task set if D i ≤ T i holds for each task τ i . Otherwise, it is an arbitrary-deadline task set. In this paper, we focus on constrained-deadline task sets.

We consider partitioned multi-core scheduling in this paper. That is, each task is statically assigned onto a core. Furthermore, we assume that a fixed-priority scheduling policy is adopted to preemptively schedule the tasks assigned to a core. Without loss of generality, we assume that the priority of task τ i is higher than the priority of task τ j if i < j. In contrast to the preemptively scheduling policy on a core, the memory access request of a task τ i may be blocked if the requested memory bank is currently processing another memory request of a lower priority task. In this case, τ i needs to wait at most η time units when its memory access request is blocked, while the maximum blocking time that τ i may encounter is at most σ i η. Since a memory segment contains at least a memory access request which takes at most η time units, we assume that σ i η ≤ A i . We define the problem as follows: Definition 1. The Memory Bank Partitioning (MBP) problem: This problem considers a multi-core platform that consists of m homogeneous cores and coupled with P single-port memory banks, each of which contains B blocks of memory. A task is characterized by a 7-tuple (m i , C i , A i , a j i , T i , D i , σ i ) and a 2-tuple (A i , σ i ) on each memory bank . Given a task set T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , • • • , τ n } of n independent tasks, we need to determine a task partition and a bank partition so that the real-time constraint and the memory capacity constraint of the task set are both conformed.

For the MBP problem, we say that a schedule of a task set is feasible if the real-time constraint and the memory capacity constraint of the task set are both conformed. A task set is deemed schedulable by an algorithm if the resulting schedule satisfies the real-time constraint and the memory capacity constraint of the task set. A schedulability test related to a specific task model is used to validate if a task set is schedulable by a particular scheduling algorithm. The demand bound function [1] dbf i (t) is employed to calculate the upper bound of cumulative execution time for a task τ i and any real number t ≥ 0. Specifically, dbf i (t) counts cumulative execution time of all jobs that task τ i can generate and the deadlines and arrival times of the jobs are within a contiguous time interval of length t. Given that a time interval of length t, we define the demand bound function for task τ i on a computing core to be dbf C i (t) = max(0, ( t-Di Ti + 1) × C i ), while for task τ i on memory access dbf A i (t) = max(0, ( t-Di Ti + 1) × A i ).

div.head: C. Resource Augmentation Technique
div.p: In this paper, we develop efficient algorithms for the problem under consideration with the idea of resource augmentation [14], [20], such as faster processors, or larger memory space. Through the analysis of an algorithm developed with resource augmentation, we can quantify resource augmentation factor(s), which can be useful in terms of system synthesis or a schedulability test. In what follows, unless otherwise stated, we use a speedup factor to denote how fast a processor should be sped up, while a memory augmentation factor to indicate how large memory space should be expanded. From the perspective of system synthesis, given a feasible task set, we can understand the amount of resources required to make it schedulable by the developed algorithm. On the other hand, from the perspective of a schedulability test, we can quantify the failure of a sufficient schedulability test.

Suppose we have an algorithm Π with a speedup factor of . If a given task set is feasible, the algorithm Π can then yield a schedulable task partitioning of the task set by accelerating times CPU speed. In contrast, the contrapositive statement is that a given task set is deemed infeasible on a platform with CPU speed decelerated times if the task set is not schedulable by the algorithm Π. In the context of this paper, we develop an algorithm with both a speedup factor of α and a memory augmentation factor of β. From the system synthesis perspective, given a feasible task set, the algorithm can yield a schedulable task partitioning of the task set by accelerating times CPU speed and augmenting β times the capacity of each memory bank. Other than this, if the dependence of α and β can be further exploited, system developers can then draw an idea concerning how to trade hardware costs off for performance or the other way around.

div.head: III. RESPONSE-TIME ANALYSIS A. Overview
div.p: In this paper, the schedulability of a task τ k is evaluated under the assumption in which all tasks with priority higher than τ k are deemed schedulable. Such an assumption can be realized if we examine the schedulability of each task in the task set in accordance with task priority one by one. Without loss of generality, we now proceed with the focus of an RAS task τ k in the sequel. Given an RAS task τ k , it is deemed schedulable if we can derive an upper bound R k of τ k 's worst-case response time and make sure that the bound R k is not more than D k . We assume that the priority of each task is known a priori, and denote the set of tasks with priority higher than the task τ k as hp(k).

When it comes to task partitioning onto cores or memory banks, we employ the following notations to ease the presentation. The core to which the task τ k is statically assigned is denoted as core q. The set of tasks assigned to core q is denoted as Γ q . In addition, as the result of data partitioning for a task τ k , each memory request of the task τ k is statically tied to a memory bank. We use Λ to denote the set of tasks that allocate data either in whole or in part on memory bank . Therefore, tasks in the set hp(k) ∩ Γ q can interfere the execution of task τ k on core q, while tasks in the set hp(k) ∩ Λ can interfere the processing of memory requests of task τ k on memory bank .

In the following, we brief the idea of symmetric responsetime analysis, which is developed to bound R k of an RAS task τ k , in Section III-B, while the idea of a rectified analysis to a platform equipped with multiple memory banks in Section III-C. The improvement to the schedulability of a task set is expected through the introduction of distributing data accesses among memory banks. Nevertheless, to make possible such an improvement, task data partitioning among multiple memory banks still needs a careful design. As an exploratory investigation, we analyze the speedup factor of an arbitrary data partitioning in Section III-D and draw insights for a better data partitioning strategy accordingly.

div.head: B. Symmetric Analysis for Single Memory Bank
div.p: Huang et al. [12] propose a symmetric way to conduct realtime analysis for RAS tasks. The timing analysis is designed from a core-centric perspective and a shared-resource-centric perspective. In terms of the core-centric perspective (resp. shared-resource-centric perspective), a task is said ready if it is either executed on a core ( resp. processing a memory request) or waited in a ready queue. The work [12] names the task executed/suspended on the core cexecution/c-suspension from the core-centric perspective. Correspondingly, it is respectively called r-suspension/rexecution from the shared-resource-centric perspective. In the following, unless stated otherwise, we adopt the sharedresource-centric perspective by default. Due to the fact that a task is either ready to be executed on a core or ready to access memory banks, the strategy proposed to bound R k in [12] is to respectively derive the r-suspension time S k (t) and the r-execution time X k (t) within a given time period t. In this way, the smallest t that satisfies
div.formula: S k (t) + X k (t) ≤ t is a safe upper bound to R k .
div.p: Specifically, the r-suspension time S k (t) of task τ k executed statically on core q within a time period t is at most

div.p: In what follows, we proceed to adapt the symmetric analysis (the r-execution time X k (t) in particular) to the systems equipped with multiple memory banks. When the data required by task τ k spreads among memory banks, we denote the upper bound of the time spent on accessing memory bank without any interference as A k , while the maximum number of memory access segments on memory bank as σ k . Note that, the exact figures of A k and σ k on memory bank is dependent on the task data partitioning and, thus, can not be determined a priori. On the other hand, the memory access interference from a higher-priority task τ i assigned to the memory bank is now defined as E i (t) = t+Ri Ti A i . As for core partitioning, any reasonable fitting algorithms [10], such as first-fit, bestfit, or worst-fit, can be applied to partition tasks onto cores. The tasks are prioritized in a deadline-monotonic order. In Theorem 1, we analyze the speedup factor for such an arbitrary memory partitioning while employing symmetric response time analysis. From the above analysis, a solution derived by arbitrary memory bank partitioning is generally unbounded in the extreme case, e.g., the number P of banks in a system is ∞. Two observations are found to design a better memory partitioning strategy. First, we should limit the maximum number (i.e., φ) of banks among which the data requested within each memory access segment of task τ k may spread. To ease the readability, we dub this internal data spreading. Second, in order to mitigate memory access interferences (the second term in Equation ( 7) ), we should endeavor to spread the data allocation of different tasks among banks. We dub this external data spreading. In summary, the avoidance of the internal data spreading can depress the number of memory access blocking, while the advocacy of the external data spreading reduce the number of higher-priority tasks that may interfere task τ k .

div.head: IV. TASK PARTITIONING WITH MEMORY AUGMENTATION A. Overview
div.p: The memory interferences to a task τ k comes from higherpriority tasks sharing a memory bank with τ k , while the memory access blocking to a task τ k comes from the lower priority tasks sharing a memory bank with τ k . From the external-data-spreading observation drawn in Section III-D, we are suggested that the less number of data splits of τ k among different memory banks, the less incurred memory interferences from other tasks. Likewise, from the internal-data-spreading observation drawn in Section III-D, we should limit the data partitioning among banks for a task. In this section, we further propose two ideas to devise a partitioning algorithm. First, the idea of dedicated memory banks: if a memory bank is dedicated to a task, the task incurs no blocking from lower-priority tasks and no memory interference from higher-priority tasks on the bank. Second, the idea of prioritized task partitioning: if we partition tasks in accordance with the priority levels, the last task partitioned to a specific memory bank incurs no blocking from lower-priority tasks due to the fact that it is the lowest priority task on the bank.

Stemming from the observations and ideas, we propose a two-phase task partitioning algorithm in Section IV-B. Besides, we incorporate the idea of memory augmentation in the partitioning algorithm. (The amount of memory augmentation is configurable by users.) In this way, the schedulability of the proposed algorithm may be further improved when the memory capacity can be augmented. We provide the analysis of the resource augmentation factors of the proposed algorithm in Section IV-C. In the analysis, we capture the relation between the CPU speedup factor and the memory augmentation factor. Being aware of such relation, we can help system developers to understand the tradeoff between hardware costs and performance. In Section IV-D, given a feasible task set, we explain how the proposed algorithm can be employed to derive a schedulable solution requiring the least amount of memory augmentation.

div.head: B. Task Partitioning Algorithm
div.p: We devise a two-phase algorithm based on the observations and ideas mentioned in Section IV-A to partition tasks onto memory banks. In the first phase, we endeavor to mitigate internal data spreading by using the idea of dedicated memory banks. Since the data size of a task may be larger than that of a memory bank, we first allocate some empty banks, each of which is dedicated to a task with data size greater than B. Afterwards, the data size of each yet-tobe-partitioned task is less than B. In the second phase, we endeavor to promote external data spreading together with the idea of prioritized task partitioning. We employ a worstfit policy to partition tasks in accordance with the priority levels to a memory bank * with the least sum of memory interference. That is, * = argmin

If we partition a task to a memory bank, say bank * , on which the number of available blocks is less than the data size of the task, we have to select another memory bank to accommodate the rest unallocated data of the task. Note that, as we mentioned in the second observation, the task incurs no blocking time on bank * . In Section IV-C, we will prove that such a design incurs a bounded number of memory access blocking. Unfortunately, impeded by the constraint of the memory bank capacity, we can not always select a memory bank with the least memory interferences to task τ k . Moreover, as astute readers may point out, the incurred memory interferences due to data splitting of task τ k may result in excessive response time R k and, thus, fail the schedulability test more easily. To deal with such a concern, we design our task partition algorithm with the incorporation of a memory augmentation idea. Specifically, the capacity of each memory bank is now assumed to be (1 + γ)B, where γ ≥ 0. In this way, we can help system developers to tradeoff between hardware costs and performance. The analysis of the speedup factor and memory augmentation factor of the proposed algorithm is provided in Section IV-C. Procedure FRACTIONALALLOCATION Algorithm 1 shows the proposed two-phase algorithm, which is named Interference-Minimized Algorithm with Resource Augmentation consideration (abbreviated to IMA-RA). The task set is assigned in a deadline monotonic order so that we can assure that a task with shorter deadline has a better chance to be assigned to a bank with the least sum of memory interference. Recall that, the employed schedulability test calculates the execution time on CPU and the processing time on memory separately, i.e., the rsuspension time and the r-execution time. Thus, we partition each task of the task set onto cores and memory banks separately. To minimize the r-suspension time of a task τ k , a straightforward idea is to allocate the task onto a core where the higher priority tasks cause the minimum sum of interferences to the task τ k . To this end, we employ a worstfit policy to partition the tasks onto cores. The steps of the algorithm are detailed as follows: In Step 3, we maintain a variable, banks, to keep track of memory banks that have available blocks. In Step 4, we first invoke the procedure IntegralAllocation to conduct the first phase of memory bank partitioning. In Steps 6-10, for each task τ k ∈ T , we select a core with minimum interferences of higher-priority tasks to task τ k by using Equation (1) under the condition t = D k , and assign task τ k to the core. In Step 8, we then invoke the procedure FractionalAllocation to conduct the second phase of memory bank partitioning. In Step 9, we check to see if τ k is schedulable with the core partitioning and memory bank partitioning. Lastly, the core partition and the bank partition are returned in Step 11, if the given task set is schedulable. In what follows, we focus our attention on the two phases for memory bank partitioning.

div.p: Phase 1: IntegralAllocation: Procedure IntegralAllocation details the first phase of the memory bank partitioning algorithm. In Step 1, we use a variable bankIndex to keep track of the starting index of available memory banks. In the loop from Step 2 to Step 10, we check the data size of each task τ k in the task set, and allocate an entire bank to a task if necessary. First, we calculate the required number of memory banks that task τ k can allocate data entirely in Step 3. If the required number of memory banks for task τ k is greater than 0, then we select the exact number of free banks in Step 5, allocate the data of task τ k to fulfill these banks, and update the management counters and the remaining unallocated data size in Steps 6-10. Recall that, the sum of the data size of the task set is less than or equal to the sum of memory banks, P B. Therefore, we are free from the deficiency of available banks. The time complexity for this procedure is O(nP ).

Phase 2: FractionalAllocation: Let us start with a brief explanation of the design idea in the second phase. We say that a memory bank is full if the available memory blocks of the bank are used up. If a bank is not full after we allocate the data of a task to the bank, then the data allocation is valid. Otherwise, we first allocate the data to the bank until it is full and choose another bank with the least memory interferences to task τ k so as to allocate the rest data. Such a process is repeated if the later chosen memory bank becomes full as well and some of task τ k 's data is not allocated yet. If task τ k is allocated to a bank without data splitting, then the memory interference to the task comes from all the higher-priority tasks assigned to this bank. If task τ k needs to be split to allocate data on memory banks, the memory interference to the task comes from all the higher-priority tasks assigned to those banks. In addition, since a task with split data allocation makes the banks accommodating task τ k (but not the last bank) become full, these banks, thus, will not be involved in the bank partitioning of the following tasks. In other words, the memory interference of each higher-priority task is counted at most once to task τ k in Equation (5). div.head: C. Resource Augmentation Factor Analysis
div.p: In this section, we first analyze the upper bound of the blocking time for each task τ k in the task set, and then conclude this section by a proof of the speedup factor and memory augmentation factor for the IMA-RA algorithm. Lemma 3. By employing Algorithm 1, the blocking time for each task τ k in the task set is at most σ k η.

Proof: As mentioned earlier, task data allocated in the first phase of memory partitioning incurs no blocking from lower-priority tasks. (There is no other tasks partitioned on the bank dedicated to a particular task.) In the second phase of memory partitioning, the data of a task τ k may be allocated on a bank in whole or in part. Suppose that task τ k 's data is allocated on a bank in whole. Due to the fact that τ k only access a memory bank that potentially other lower-priority tasks might be co-located and, thus, the blocking time for the task is at most σ k η. On the other hand, suppose that task τ k 's data is allocated on several banks in part. Recall that, in the algorithm, we partition tasks onto banks one-by-one by following task priority, and task data is allocated in part only when the number of available blocks on the bank designated is less than the data size of the task. Following this track, only the last memory bank that has enough available blocks to accommodate the remaining unallocated data of task τ k could potentially accommodate lower-priority tasks. In this way, we can conclude that the blocking time for the task is at most σ k η as well.

div.head: D. Remarks
div.p: In this section, we start with a few examples to demonstrate how the analysis in Section IV-C can be applied by system developers. Then, we conclude the section by providing a bisection algorithm that can be employed to derive a schedulable solution requiring the least amount of memory augmentation. Assume that
div.formula: P =1 A k ≤ ρA k . That is, ρ = 1.
div.p: Suppose we are given γ = 1. We can make a task set, which is feasible in the original platform, schedulable by speeding up the platform 14 times and augmenting each memory banks 2 times. As a comparison, given γ = ∞, we can make a task set, which is feasible in the original platform, schedulable by speeding up the platform 11 times and augmenting each memory banks ∞ times.

Algorithm 2 shows a bisection method to derive a solution with the least memory augmentation. The algorithm is named Interference-Minimized Algorithm with the Least Resource Augmentation (abbreviated to IMA-LRA). First, we set an upper bound and a lower bound of the tested capacity for each memory bank in Steps 2-3. Note that, since the sum of data size of the task set is less than or equal to P B, we configure the upper bound to P B. In Step 4, we configure the additional memory augmentation number γ to -∞ so that we can be aware of the outcome of the first test point by examine γ. In Step 5, we declare a variable budget to keep track of the bank capacity we are going to test at the moment. In the loop from Step 6 to Step 20, we repeatedly invoke the IMA-RA algorithm with different budget. In Step 7, we employ γ as a temporary variable, and configure it to be the additional memory augmentation number. In Steps 8-9, we stop the test if γ is less than 0 or the test points in between the upper bound and the lower bound is running out. We then invoke the IMA-RA algorithm in Step 10, and test the schedulability of the given task set according to the returned task partitioning in the loop in Step 11. If the task set is schedulable, we proceed with Step 13, assign the value of γ to γ, and update the upper test point. On the other hand, if the task set is not schedulable, we proceed with Step 16, and update the lower test point. Note that, we can stop the test directly if the tested capacity is equal to P B and the tested result is not schedulable. If the algorithm is not stopped yet, we then update the budget to be the middle point in between the latest upper bound and lower bound in Step 19. In the end, a schedulable solution with the least amount of memory augmentation is returned in Step 21. The time complexity for the IMA-LRA algorithm is O(nP2 (log P + log B)).

div.head: A. Environment Setup
div.p: The experiments were conducted on a simulated platform, which refers to the island architecture of Kalray MPPA-256 [9]. The simulated platform contains M = 8 cores and P = 8 memory banks. Each memory bank can be accessed independently, while the capacity of each memory bank is B = 128 blocks. The address mapping of the memory banks was configured as blocked mode. In the experiment, we employed synthesized task sets for the ease of evaluation. We randomly generated 5,000 task sets for each utilization level from 0.01M to 0.99M , in steps of 0.01M . The cardinality of each task set was 4 times the number of cores, i.e., n = 32. Provided a given utilization level, we adopt the UUniFast-Discard method [3] to generate task utilization values of each task set. On the other hand, as suggested by Davis et al. [7], we generate task periods according to the exponential distribution within two orders of magnitude, i.e., 10 to 1000 milliseconds. The upper bound of the total execution time on a computing core was set to period times utilization accordingly, while task relative deadlines were considered implicit, i.e., D i = T i .

On the part of resource access, we considered total access utilization levels of 0.1P and 0.3P , respectively, and generated task access utilization values of each task set by using the UUniFast method. Once the access utilization value of a task is derived, the upper bound of the time spent on local memory access for the task was set to period times the access utilization accordingly. For each task set, we ensured that the sum of total access utilization and total CPU utilization is not more than 100%. In addition, to investigate how a partition algorithm is affected by different resource access patterns, we further classified a task according to different numbers of resource access segments and different blocking time values. The maximum number of resource access segments of a task was set to 2, and 20, which corresponds to the types of rare access, and frequent access, respectively. The upper bound of blocking time η was set to 0, and 0.5 In this work, we compare the proposed algorithms with the partitioning algorithm developed in [15] and denoted as RTS2016 for brevity. The RTS2016 algorithm first builds a memory interference graph in which a node represents a task and an edge exists between any two nodes. The weight of an edge between two nodes (tasks), say τ i and τ j , is calculated by
div.formula: (Ri-Ci) Ti + (Rj -Cj ) Tj
div.p: , where the response time is yielded by assuming that the two tasks were assigned respectively to two empty cores and shared the same memory bank. In the algorithm, best-fit policy is employed for core partitioning, while a memory bank, which has the minimum sum of memory interferences between tasks already assigned to the bank and tasks unassigned, is chosen and bind to the bestfit core. For more details, we refer readers to their work [15]. The metric adopted in Y-axis to evaluate a partitioning algorithm is the acceptance ratio, which is defined as the ratio of the number of task sets deemed schedulable by an algorithm to the total number of task sets evaluated at a utilization level. On the other hand, the metric adopted in X-axis is the total CPU utilization levels normalized to the number of cores in the simulated platform. In what follows, we separately evaluate the partitioning algorithms when the blocking time η per memory access request is negligible and non-negligible, respectively.

div.head: B. Experimental Results
div.p: Figure 3 shows the experiment results of different partitioning algorithms when the blocking time per memory access request is negligible (e.g., 0 ms). Specifically, we first investigate the results when the memory is not augmented in Figures 3(a) and 3(b), and then the results when memory augmentation is applied in Figures 3(c) and 3(d). As can be seen from Figures 3(a) and 3(b), the partitioning algorithm IMA-RA proposed in this paper improved the schedulability significantly when compared with the RTS2016 partitioning algorithm. Now, let's proceed to investigate the case when memory augmentation is allowed, as shown in 3(c) and 3(d). When the memory was augmented by 10%, 25%, and 50%, we can see that the schedulability improvement for IMA-RA is only slightly, but profoundly for RTS2016. This is due to the lack of capacity limitation in the RTS2016 design, so a task may be partitioned to a memory bank that is out of available blocks already. This also explained that the schedulability was significantly improved when the memory was augmented. When the memory was augmented by 50%, the RTS2016 algorithm even outperformed the proposed algorithm IMA-RA. One interesting phenomenon is that, when the memory is augmented by 25%, the schedulability results of the RTS2016 algorithm was low initially, but improved in the middle of normalized CPU utilization levels. This is due to the core-bank binding design of the RTS2016 algorithm.

Figures 4 and5 show the experiment results of different partitioning algorithms when the blocking time per memory access request is non-negligible (e.g., 0.5 ms). When the blocking time per memory access request is non-negligible, we have to take the memory access types into consideration. When the memory augmentation is not allowed, as shown in Figure 4, we can see that the proposed IMA-RA algorithm outperformed the RTS2016 algorithm significantly when the considered memory access type was rare. On the other hand, both algorithms performed poorly when the the considered memory access type was frequently. Now, let's have a look at the augmented cases in Figure 5. We found that, when the considered memory access type was frequent, the RTS2016 algorithm outperformed the proposed IMA-RA algorithm. This is due to the fact, the design of the RTS2016 algorithm prohibits internal data spreading of a task (Recall that internal data spreading is mentioned in Section III-D. ) Thus, the RTS2016 algorithm may encounter less memory intereference from higher-priority tasks when memory is augmented. This property indirectly provides a better tolerance to the frequent memory access.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: In this paper, we consider to schedule RAS tasks onto a platform consisting of homogeneous cores and capacitylimited memory banks. We drew two observations from an exploratory speedup factor analysis for careless memory bank partitioning: First, we should avoid internal data spreading among memory banks for a task. Second, we should advocate external data spreading among memory banks for a given task set. Stemming from the observations, we devise a two-pahse memory partitioning algorithm with memory augmentation consideration in mind. We propose an algorithm with (4 + ρ + 3(2γ+1) γ ) speedup factor and (γ + 1) memory augmentation factor, where γ > 0 and ρ ≥ 1. The adjustable nature of the derived CPU speedup and memory augmentation factors can be useful from two different perspectives: In terms of system synthesis, we can help system developers to understand the trade-off between performance and hardware costs. On the other hand, in terms of schedulability, we could derive a schedulable solution requiring the least amount of memory augmentation under the premise that the given task set is feasible. To achieve this, a bi-section algorithm is further proposed and shoud be employed together with the two-phase algorithm. In the experiment, we conducted extensive simulations of different types of task sets and compare the experiment results with that of the RTS2016 algorithm. The proposed IMA-RA algorithm significantly outperformed the RTS2016 algorithm even when memory augmentation is prohibited.
